## Introduction

This note is a living reference: copy it to start a new note. Text, math, citations,
margin notes, and figures all work as below. Citations are numbered and show the
bibliography entry on hover [@zhang2017rethinking; @li2018visualizing].

Inline math looks like $\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \ell(f_\theta(x_i), y_i)$,
and display math can be numbered and referenced:

$$
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \, \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)
$$ {#eq-gd}

Gradient descent (@eq-gd) is the simplest optimizer.^[Footnotes go in the margin and also show on hover.]

::: {.column-margin}
**Margin note.** Any block wrapped in `.column-margin` sits in the right margin next to
the paragraph it follows.
:::

## Figures at three widths

Hover over a figure reference to preview the figure: @fig-curves shows a body-width
figure, @fig-grid a page-width one, and @fig-wide a full-screen one. Click a figure to zoom.

::: {#fig-curves}
```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
from plotting import plot_curves, plot_grid
plot_curves("results/curves.csv")
```

Body width. Training and validation loss (made-up numbers).
:::

::: {#fig-grid .column-page}
```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
plot_grid("results/grid.csv", xlabel="item popularity (train interactions)", ylabel="user history")
```

Page width (`.column-page`). Share of test interactions by user history and item popularity.
:::

::: {#fig-wide .column-screen}
```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
plot_curves("results/curves.csv", figsize=(14, 3.2))
```

Screen width (`.column-screen`). The same curves, as wide as the window.
:::

A figure can also have its caption in the margin:

::: {#fig-margin-cap cap-location="margin"}
```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
plot_curves("results/curves.csv")
```

A caption placed in the margin with `cap-location="margin"`.
:::

## Code

Code chunks that produce figures are hidden (`echo: false`). To *show* code, use a
plain code block; it gets a copy button. This is how every figure above is written: the
label, width class, and caption go on a `:::` block, and the chunk only plots.
`renderings: [light, dark]` makes Quarto show the version that matches the page theme
(the plotting functions draw both).

````markdown
::: {#fig-curves .column-page}
```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
from plotting import plot_curves
plot_curves("results/curves.csv")
```

Caption text, which can cite [@zhang2017rethinking].
:::
````
